Question: I've read Kendokas saying they don't do hard parries with katanas, but why do I see a lot of hard parry in the Kenjutsu sparring video of Weaponism (YouTuber)?
Answer: Kendo generally does not do a hard parry. In fact, I’d be pressed to recall too many times that hard, strong, or other similar adjectives applied. Of course, there are times when hard or strong do apply. Like when some dude using Jo-dan gets you hard on the wrist with the point of their shinai. Ouch! Or when you get hit hard on the forearm or just above the body armor on the side. There’s also strong when the two fighters come together in taiatari, but these are expected. You just go with it. The parry is usually a quick flick with the end of the shinai or a kind of a wrist twist parry with the meat of the shinai. Either way, it isn’t hard, quick and firm would be better descriptors. A hard parry would likely leave an opening for another attack. Kendo is much more about speed, quickness, anticipation, and reaction than about strength and power. The dudes that are really good are lightening fast in their reactions. Any opening given and they are on you in a blink of an eye. Many years ago the college team I practiced with went to Kanazawa University for a visit. Eto Sensei of Kanazawa Dai was all Japan champion twice(?) and second twice(?). Now that dude was hella quick. He could double hit you on the body, left - right, so fast it didn’t really make sense. And his kote, oh my! I mean, Eto Sensei would go kote, men, back off, then give you the double do. FAST! He’d be doing this to the college seniors; guys with years and years of kendo. Amazing. Anyhoo, I think that a hard parry is something unnecessary.

Question: In WWII, when Japanese soldiers yelled “banzai” by itself, was this specifically a reference to the emperor?
Answer: My understanding is that the term, “banzai” had a connection the Emperor, but that when shouting it during an attack, thoughts of the Emperor were not foremost in the mind. Many nations and armies had and have things they shouted to keep up their spirits in trying times. “Banzai” was used in a similar way.

Question: In baseball games, my bat can never make contact with the ball. I have fine power and in practice with slower pitches I do fine. How do I fix this?
Answer: When reading the question, the following stood out to me: “I have fine power and in practice with slower pitches I do fine”. This makes me think that you are trying to ‘hit for power’. I would suggest that you try to swing for contact. This may well involve opening your stance and changes in your bat angles. Once you’ve gotten to the point of making good contact then you can slowly add in the power. If you aren’t making contact, power is meaningless. Good luck and keep your head in.
